title: Black Forest Well Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Black Forest wells have a median depth of 315 ft. Compare local yields, water levels, permit history and finished-well costs of $21,800-$34,000.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Black Forest
intro_html:
A Black Forest well budget starts with the aquifer beneath the lot, not just the house plans. Nearby records show a median well depth of 315 feet and a median reported yield of 11.0 gpm. Those are useful starting points, but neither guarantees what a particular parcel will produce.

This summary covers Colorado DWR permit records within 5 miles of Black Forest in El Paso County. Use it to frame a bid, then narrow the comparison to wells near the property.

sections.heading: Budget for Black Forest’s Typical Depth, Not Its Shallowest Well
sections.html:
The middle half of reported well depths runs from 275 to 395 feet, with a median of 315 feet. That spread matters when comparing bids: a quote based only on the median needs clear terms for additional drilling, casing and completion work. The 90th-percentile depth is 480 feet, so deeper work is part of the local record.

Black Forest drilling is in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. Dawson is named on 4,310 permits and Denver on 206; many records lack a specific aquifer name. Aquifer depth, ground elevation and the permitted completion target help determine the finished depth. Records toward Gleneagle or Peyton are useful context, but the closest comparable aquifer completions deserve more weight.

sections.heading: Reported Black Forest Yields Cluster Around Household Supply
sections.html:
Among the 3,580 records reporting pump yield, the median is 11.0 gpm and the middle half runs from 9.0 to 12.8 gpm. That fairly tight middle range gives a buyer a useful benchmark for evaluating a seller’s well test. It does not establish how long an individual well can sustain that output.

The reported share under 1 gpm is 0%, while 1% falls in the 1–5 gpm band. Those figures do not rule out weak or unsuccessful wells outside the yield-reporting records. Ask for a current pumping and recovery test. Also read the permit: physical capacity does not authorize lawn irrigation, livestock watering or other uses beyond its terms.

sections.heading: Black Forest Water Levels Do Not Show a Steady Decline
sections.html:
Static water level is the resting depth to water, not the drilled depth or the level during pumping. The 606 records with this measurement have a median of 132 feet below ground; the middle half is 85–187 feet. A driller needs both the completion details and pumping response to plan pump placement.

Decade medians were 138 feet in the 1970s, 150 feet in the 2000s and 120 feet in the 2020s. This series does not show a steady drop in the water table. It also does not prove recovery: these are grouped measurements from potentially different wells and aquifers, not repeated monitoring of the same well.

sections.heading: A Long Permit History, With Dawson Prominent in the Records
sections.html:
The search area contains 6,919 DWR permit records, with 4,638 recorded as constructed. Permit counts are not a count of functioning wells today. Issuance rose from 602 in the 1970s to 1,467 in the 1990s. The newest permit year is 2026; the 509 permits in the 2020s represent an unfinished decade.

The most active drillers in these records are Kunau Drilling Llc with 1,399, Fletcher Drilling with 1,024, and Hamacher Well Works Inc with 729. These are historical record counts, not current availability or recommendations. Domestic/household use appears on 94% of permits, making the records particularly relevant to residential buyers.

sections.heading: A Finished Black Forest Well Costs More Than the Hole
sections.html:
The local cost model uses $50–$70 per foot for drilling Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 315-foot median depth, the drilled hole is approximately $15,800–$22,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $21,800–$34,000.

Treat those figures as a planning range, not a parcel-specific quote. The 275–395-foot middle depth range alone leaves room for meaningful bid differences. Ask each driller to identify the assumed aquifer and depth, casing and grout scope, pump equipment, and trench route. Confirm how additional depth, difficult access and an unsuccessful completion would be charged. A low drilling-only price is not directly comparable with a complete water-system proposal.

sections.heading: Check Water Quality and Completion Risk Before Closing
sections.html:
Within about 10 miles, mapped environmental records include 31 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 4 historic mine features and 2 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites. These are screening flags, not evidence that a particular Black Forest well is contaminated. Sampling sites may represent investigation rather than a confirmed problem at your property.

Have the well water tested rather than relying on taste, clarity or the seller’s experience. Ask a qualified laboratory or local health authority which tests fit the location, including whether PFAS testing is warranted. Review casing, grout and wellhead condition alongside septic placement and drainage. For a new well, discuss low-yield or unsuccessful-hole contingencies; a favorable neighborhood yield summary cannot eliminate that risk.

sections.heading: Fit the Black Forest Lot Plan Around the Well and Septic
sections.html:
Before buying, match the property’s permit to its construction record, pump information and authorized uses. For an existing home, request a current yield and recovery test plus water-quality results. For vacant land, establish the DWR permitting path before treating a neighboring well as proof that your proposed use is allowed. An exempt household-use permit should not be assumed to cover outdoor demands.

Lay out the well, septic system, house, driveway and utility trench together. Leave practical access for the drilling rig and future pump service. Compare nearby completions on the Black Forest side of Monument, Woodmoor or Falcon only where aquifer and terrain conditions are comparable. Town proximity alone is a poor basis for a drilling budget.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Black Forest, Colorado?
faq.a: Within 5 miles of Black Forest, reported wells have a median depth of 315 feet. The middle half runs from 275 to 395 feet, and the 90th-percentile depth is 480 feet. Use that range when requesting bids, then check nearby wells completed in the same aquifer rather than assuming the median fits your lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Black Forest?
faq.a: The local model puts drilling at $50–$70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 315-foot median depth, the hole costs about $15,800–$22,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $21,800–$34,000. Actual bids depend on completion depth, equipment, access and the utility route.

faq.q: How much water do Black Forest wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 11.0 gpm, with the middle half between 9.0 and 12.8 gpm. These figures come from 3,580 yield-reporting records. They provide a useful comparison for a property’s test results, but do not guarantee sustained output. Get a pumping and recovery test and confirm that the permit allows your intended uses.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Black Forest?
faq.a: Safety needs to be established by testing the individual well. Nearby mapping identifies 31 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 4 historic mine features and 2 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those counts do not establish contamination at your home. Review well construction and septic conditions, and ask a qualified laboratory about appropriate testing.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Black Forest?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a steady decline. Static water depth was 138 feet in the 1970s, 150 feet in the 2000s and 120 feet in the 2020s. However, these grouped records are not a same-well monitoring series. They cannot establish a long-term trend for the aquifer serving a particular property.
